title: SafeSport Will Now Alert Schools, Clubs if Coaches Sanctioned for Abuse Continue to Work With Kids
author: Molly Hensley-Clancy
content:
The U.S. Center for SafeSport is taking steps to stop coaches banned over
allegations of sexual abuse from working with children, part of an initiative
that the organization said it is launching because of [reporting by ProPublica
and The Washington Post](https://www.propublica.org/article/aau-youth-sports-
sexual-abuse-failure-amateur-athletic-union) about [gaps in the child
protection](https://www.propublica.org/article/ryan-richardson-pharr-texas-
usa-volleyball-safesport-abuse-teens) system in youth sports.

Charged by Congress with investigating allegations of sexual abuse in sports,
SafeSport has the power to suspend or permanently bar coaches from contact
with athletes and place their names on a [public disciplinary
list](https://cdd.uscenterforsafesport.org/). But the center has authority
only over the country’s national sports governing bodies, which are overseen
by the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee. Elementary and high schools,
colleges and many independent youth sports leagues are not required to follow
SafeSport’s bans, though some opt to do so. Parents and other caregivers only
know if a coach has been sanctioned if they check the list.

SafeSport’s new initiative encourages people to find and report banned coaches
who are continuing to work with children, SafeSport said, with a publicity
initiative that includes [a video with its
CEO](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=1Dft3Hxh5Ns).

It is also launching a new “internal process” to notify schools and other
organizations that coaches are on the SafeSport list. Hilary Nemchik,
SafeSport’s vice president of external affairs, said the organization would
send a form letter when it learned coaches were still working with kids,
either as a result of its own investigation or in response to a report.

“When SafeSport imposes a sanction for abuse or misconduct, the community
should be aware,” Benita Fitzgerald Mosley, SafeSport’s CEO, said in a
statement. “Someone could be on the SafeSport Database for abuse but go on to
work at a school or coach for a league outside of our jurisdiction.”

ProPublica and The Post discovered several coaches who had been banned by
SafeSport but continued to work with children. One story [highlighted the case
of a volleyball coach](https://www.propublica.org/article/ryan-richardson-
pharr-texas-usa-volleyball-safesport-abuse-teens), Ryan Richardson, who
SafeSport found to have committed sexual misconduct with a minor but who has
continued coaching teenage girls in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas. An
independent volleyball league allowed Richardson to coach at several of its
tournaments even after his name appeared on SafeSport’s database. Videos
posted online showed Richardson on the sidelines.

The reporting showed that Richardson continued coaching in part by allowing a
former assistant, Gavin Rudder, to take over the volleyball club after
Richardson was banned by USA Volleyball, the sport’s governing body, in 2024.
ProPublica and The Post found that Rudder allowed Richardson to coach the
teams for years after the ban, a violation of the SafeSport code.

After the story was published, SafeSport added Rudder’s name to its public
database, listing him as temporarily restricted from unsupervised coaching or
training.

Rudder is [currently listed](https://www.maxpreps.com/tx/weslaco/weslaco-
panthers/volleyball/staff/) as the coach at Weslaco High School, near McAllen.
Abel Aguilar, the Weslaco district’s deputy superintendent, said in an email
that the district “does not comment on personnel matters.”

In a text message, Rudder said the SafeSport ban “has nothing to do with high
school volleyball” and that he had not “done anything wrong.” He said he was
no longer associated with Richardson’s club volleyball team following the end
of the 2026 season.

[ ![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/20260818-aau-
richardson-16x9-2.jpg?w=459&h=306&crop=1) **This Coach Is Banned From Working
With Kids. Why Is He Still Coaching?**
](https://www.propublica.org/article/ryan-richardson-pharr-texas-usa-
volleyball-safesport-abuse-teens)

Richardson has not responded to requests for comment on ProPublica and The
Post’s reporting. When he was first suspended in 2024 by Lone Star Region
Volleyball, the organization overseeing volleyball in South Texas, Richardson
[told](https://myrgv.com/alerts-mcm/2024/02/23/richardson-under-fire-by-usa-
volleyball/) the local news website MyRGV that complaints about him were an
effort to “retaliate and defame someone’s character,” and
[said](https://myrgv.com/rgvsports/2024/04/02/usa-volleyball-upholds-
richardson-suspension-from-coaching-training/) he “would never do anything to
risk the physical or mental wellbeing of these strong young ladies.”

In announcing the changes, SafeSport also nodded to a [bipartisan
inquiry](https://www.propublica.org/article/aau-child-sex-abuse-house-energy-
commerce-committee-probe-amateur-athletic-union) into a major youth sports
organization launched last month by the powerful House Energy and Commerce
Committee, which also oversees SafeSport.

The lawmakers said they were launching a probe of the Amateur Athletic Union
after ProPublica and The Post reported that the nonprofit does not follow
SafeSport bans and has become a [haven for coaches who are banned for
abuse](https://www.propublica.org/article/aau-youth-sports-sexual-abuse-
failure-amateur-athletic-union). The committee asked AAU President Jo Mirza
for details on its child safety policies and training, setting a deadline of
Oct. 21.

Committee representatives this week didn’t respond to questions about the
status of the investigation. The AAU, which has said in a statement that it is
“committed to protecting its athletes through comprehensive protection
policies overseen by our Compliance Department,” said it would “cooperate
fully” with any inquiry.
